---
title: Preference Learning with the Pairwise GP
jupyter: python3
---

Not every objective can be read off a number line. Sometimes the only signal
available is a *comparison*: a taste panel says cake A is nicer than cake B, a
chemist judges one crystallisation cleaner than another, a user clicks one
layout over another. The quantity actually being compared — a latent *utility* —
is never observed directly.

BoFire's `PairwiseGPSurrogate` learns that latent utility from pairwise
comparison data. It wraps BoTorch's `PairwiseGP`, a Gaussian process whose
likelihood models the probability that one design is preferred over another.

This tutorial fits a pairwise GP, proposes designs with qEUBO, and shows how
to switch the same fitted strategy to qLogNEI. It finishes with a sequential BO
comparison of random and qEUBO-selected feedback pairs. No scalar utility
observations are required.

## Imports

```{python}
import warnings
from itertools import combinations

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import kendalltau

import bofire.surrogates.api as surrogates
import bofire.strategies.api as strategies
from bofire.data_models.acquisition_functions.api import qEUBO, qLogNEI
from bofire.data_models.domain.api import Domain, Inputs, Outputs
from bofire.data_models.features.api import ContinuousInput, ContinuousOutput
from bofire.data_models.likelihoods.api import PairwiseProbitLikelihood
from bofire.data_models.objectives.api import MaximizeObjective
from bofire.data_models.strategies.api import (
    BotorchOptimizer,
    PreferenceStrategy as PreferenceStrategyDataModel,
)
from bofire.data_models.surrogates.api import BotorchSurrogates, PairwiseGPSurrogate
from bofire.data_models.surrogates.optimizer import LBFGSB

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
```

## A synthetic preference problem

We work on a two-dimensional input space. The *latent utility* — the thing an
expert implicitly scores when they pick a winner — is a smooth bump that peaks
near `(0.7, 0.3)`. In a real preference experiment this function is unknown; we
define it here only so we can check what the surrogate learned.

```{python}
def latent_utility(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Ground-truth utility. Unobserved in a real preference experiment."""
    peak = np.array([0.7, 0.3])
    return -np.sum((X - peak) ** 2, axis=-1)
```

We draw a handful of candidate designs and give each a unique `labcode` — the
identifier BoFire uses to link a design to the comparisons it appears in.

```{python}
n_candidates = 40
X = rng.random((n_candidates, 2))
labcodes = [f"design_{i:02d}" for i in range(n_candidates)]

experiments = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=["x_1", "x_2"])
experiments["labcode"] = labcodes
experiments.head()
```

Now we simulate an expert comparing random pairs of designs. The expert prefers
whichever design has the higher latent utility, but their judgement is noisy, so
they occasionally pick the worse one.

```{python}
def make_comparisons(n_comparisons: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for _ in range(n_comparisons):
        i, j = rng.choice(n_candidates, size=2, replace=False)
        # noisy utilities -> the expert occasionally prefers the worse design
        u_i = latent_utility(X[i]) + rng.normal(scale=0.05)
        u_j = latent_utility(X[j]) + rng.normal(scale=0.05)
        winner, loser = (i, j) if u_i > u_j else (j, i)
        # record the winner in slot A or B at random: the *sign* of
        # `preference` carries the label, not which slot the winner sits in
        if rng.random() < 0.5:
            rows.append((labcodes[winner], labcodes[loser], 1.0))  # A preferred
        else:
            rows.append((labcodes[loser], labcodes[winner], -1.0))  # B preferred
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["labcode_A", "labcode_B", "preference"])


preferences = make_comparisons(n_comparisons=120)
preferences.head()
```

## Setting up the surrogate

A `PairwiseGPSurrogate` needs an input space and exactly one output — the latent
utility it will infer.

```{python}
inputs = Inputs(
    features=[
        ContinuousInput(key="x_1", bounds=(0.0, 1.0)),
        ContinuousInput(key="x_2", bounds=(0.0, 1.0)),
    ]
)
outputs = Outputs(
    features=[ContinuousOutput(key="utility", objective=MaximizeObjective())]
)

surrogate_data = PairwiseGPSurrogate(
    inputs=inputs,
    outputs=outputs,
    likelihood=PairwiseProbitLikelihood(),
)
surrogate = surrogates.map(surrogate_data)
```

We explicitly maximize the learned latent utility: larger values indicate
stronger preference. `MaximizeObjective()` is also the default for a
`ContinuousOutput`.

The probit likelihood is the default. To use the logistic alternative, import
`PairwiseLogitLikelihood` from `bofire.data_models.likelihoods.api` and pass
`likelihood=PairwiseLogitLikelihood()`. These likelihood data models serialize
with the surrogate configuration.

Unlike a standard surrogate, `fit` takes *two* DataFrames — the designs and the
comparisons between them:

```{python}
surrogate.fit(experiments, preferences)
surrogate.is_fitted
```

## Inspecting the learned utility

`predict` returns the posterior mean (`utility_pred`) and standard deviation
(`utility_sd`) of the latent utility on new designs. Pairwise data pins down the
*ranking* of designs, not the absolute utility values — the GP recovers utility
only up to an arbitrary scale and offset — so we score it with the Kendall-Tau
rank correlation against the true utility.

```{python}
test_X = rng.random((500, 2))
test_df = pd.DataFrame(test_X, columns=["x_1", "x_2"])
predictions = surrogate.predict(test_df)

true_utility = latent_utility(test_X)
tau = kendalltau(predictions["utility_pred"], true_utility).correlation
print(f"Kendall-Tau rank correlation vs. true utility: {tau:.3f}")
```

A correlation close to 1 means the surrogate ranks unseen designs almost exactly
as the latent utility would. We can see this directly by plotting the learned
posterior mean and standard deviation next to the ground truth. The standard
deviation shows where the model remains uncertain despite the comparisons seen
so far.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.5))

grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(grid, grid)
grid_df = pd.DataFrame({"x_1": gx.ravel(), "x_2": gy.ravel()})

true_grid = latent_utility(grid_df.to_numpy()).reshape(gx.shape)
posterior_grid = surrogate.predict(grid_df)
pred_grid = posterior_grid["utility_pred"].to_numpy().reshape(gx.shape)
sd_grid = posterior_grid["utility_sd"].to_numpy().reshape(gx.shape)

for ax, surface, title, cmap in [
    (axes[0], true_grid, "True latent utility", "viridis"),
    (axes[1], pred_grid, "Learned posterior mean", "viridis"),
    (axes[2], sd_grid, "Learned posterior standard deviation", "magma"),
]:
    contour = ax.contourf(gx, gy, surface, levels=20, cmap=cmap)
    ax.scatter(
        X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c="white", edgecolors="black", s=25,
        label="compared designs",
    )
    ax.set(xlabel="x_1", ylabel="x_2", title=title)
    fig.colorbar(contour, ax=ax)
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The true and learned mean surfaces peak in the same region: from comparisons
alone, the surrogate has located where utility is highest. The absolute mean
values differ — pairwise learning identifies the latent utility only up to an
arbitrary scale and offset — but the *ranking*, which is what matters for
optimization, is recovered. The standard-deviation panel is largest in regions
that are weakly informed by the observed comparisons.

## The preference encoding

The `preferences` DataFrame must have exactly these three columns:

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `labcode_A` | first design in the comparison (must appear in `experiments`) |
| `labcode_B` | second design in the comparison (must appear in `experiments`) |
| `preference` | `1` → A preferred, `-1` → B preferred, `0` → tie |

The value must be exactly `-1`, `0`, or `1`. Tied rows are dropped with a
warning. Because the slot (A vs. B) is just bookkeeping, swapping `labcode_A`
with `labcode_B` and flipping `preference` describes the very same comparison
and yields the same fit.

## Proposing a comparison with qEUBO

`PreferenceStrategy` combines the pairwise GP with acquisition optimization.
Its default acquisition, [qEUBO](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v206/astudillo23a.html),
maximizes the expected latent utility of the best member of a proposed batch.
It defaults to two designs for a preference query. This favors promising
comparisons; it does not directly maximize information gain.

```{python}
domain = Domain(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)
strategy_data = PreferenceStrategyDataModel(
    domain=domain,
    surrogate_specs=BotorchSurrogates(surrogates=[surrogate_data]),
    acquisition_function=qEUBO(n_mc_samples=64),
    acquisition_optimizer=BotorchOptimizer(
        n_restarts=4, n_raw_samples=128, maxiter=200,
    ),
    seed=42,
)
strategy = strategies.map(strategy_data)
strategy.tell(experiments, preferences=preferences)
next_pair = strategy.ask()  # qEUBO defaults to two designs
next_pair
```

Omitting `surrogate_specs` creates a default pairwise GP. If supplied, the
collection must contain exactly one `PairwiseGPSurrogate`.

## Switching acquisitions on the same fitted model

Each strategy instance has **one active acquisition function**. Change the
runtime strategy's `acquisition_function` to reuse its fitted GP, designs, and
comparisons. There is no need to construct another strategy or refit the model.

```{python}
# Propose one new design using improvement in the inferred utility.
strategy.acquisition_function = qLogNEI(n_mc_samples=64)
next_experiment = strategy.ask()  # qLogNEI defaults to one design
next_experiment
```

qLogNEI integrates over uncertain baseline utilities, so it needs no observed
scalar utility or known incumbent value. Its proposed design still needs a
comparison partner before it can supply preference feedback.

Switching back also changes the acquisition used by `calc_acquisition`. This
method scores supplied designs without optimizing over the domain:

```{python}
strategy.acquisition_function = qEUBO(n_mc_samples=64)
measured_pair = experiments.iloc[[0, 1]][inputs.get_keys()]
pair_value = strategy.calc_acquisition(measured_pair, combined=True)
print(f"qEUBO value of this measured pair: {pair_value.item():.3f}")
```

`combined=True` scores the two rows as one batch. This is useful in a workflow
that uses qLogNEI to propose experiments and qEUBO to score comparisons among
measured designs. Selecting comparison partners and deciding when to switch
acquisitions remain choices for the calling code.

| Acquisition | Criterion | Default designs from `ask()` |
|---|---|---|
| `qEUBO` | Expected utility of the best batch member | 2 |
| `qLogNEI` | Expected improvement over the uncertain baseline, in log space | 1 |
| `qSR` | Expected utility of the best batch member | 1 |
| `qUCB` | Upper confidence bound, controlled by `beta` | 1 |

All four are imported from `bofire.data_models.acquisition_functions.api`.
`ask(candidate_count=...)` requests a larger batch; qEUBO requires at least two
designs. For identical batches and posterior samples, qSR and qEUBO have the
same value; for one design, that criterion reduces to posterior mean utility.

## Recording the next preference

Give the proposed qEUBO pair unique labcodes, obtain the expert's judgment, and
append both the designs and comparison with `tell`. Here we simulate the judgment
using the hidden utility:

```{python}
new_experiments = next_pair[inputs.get_keys()].copy()
new_experiments["labcode"] = ["query_A", "query_B"]
noisy_utility = latent_utility(
    new_experiments[inputs.get_keys()].to_numpy()
) + rng.normal(scale=0.05, size=2)
new_preferences = pd.DataFrame(
    [("query_A", "query_B", 1 if noisy_utility[0] > noisy_utility[1] else -1)],
    columns=["labcode_A", "labcode_B", "preference"],
)
strategy.tell(new_experiments, preferences=new_preferences)
```

`tell` appends data and refits by default. Use `replace=True` to replace both
tables, or pass an empty experiment DataFrame when adding only comparisons
between designs already known to the strategy.

Generate initial designs with `domain.inputs.sample(...)` or a standalone
`RandomStrategy`, collect comparisons, and pass both tables to
`PreferenceStrategy.tell`. Preference strategies cannot be used as steps in
`StepwiseStrategy`.

## Comparing feedback policies in a BO loop

We now compare **random pairs** with **qEUBO-selected pairs**. Both policies
start from four random designs and two comparisons. Each BO round uses qLogNEI
to propose one new experiment, then spends the same budget of two comparisons
among all measured designs. Only the feedback-selection policy differs.

This separates experiment acquisition from feedback acquisition: a measured
outcome can be compared with earlier outcomes without running another
experiment. The latent utility is used only to simulate judgments and score
progress; the optimizer receives comparisons throughout.

```{python}
N_INITIAL = 4
N_STEPS = 10
N_REPLICATES = 10
N_COMPARISONS = 2

# Keep the repeated GP fits small; use the same configuration in both arms.
study_data = strategy_data.model_copy(deep=True)
study_data.acquisition_function = qLogNEI(n_mc_samples=64)
study_data.surrogate_specs.surrogates[0].optimizer = LBFGSB(maxiter=50)


def label_pairs(designs, pairs, noise_rng):
    rows = []
    for a, b in pairs:
        pair = designs.iloc[[a, b]]
        utility = latent_utility(pair[inputs.get_keys()].to_numpy())
        utility += noise_rng.normal(scale=0.03, size=2)
        rows.append(
            (
                pair.iloc[0]["labcode"],
                pair.iloc[1]["labcode"],
                1 if utility[0] > utility[1] else -1,
            )
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["labcode_A", "labcode_B", "preference"])


def run_bo(feedback, replicate):
    pair_rng = np.random.default_rng(10_000 + replicate)
    noise_rng = np.random.default_rng(20_000 + replicate)
    designs = inputs.sample(N_INITIAL, seed=replicate)
    designs["labcode"] = [f"measurement_{i}" for i in range(N_INITIAL)]
    pairs = list(combinations(range(N_INITIAL), 2))
    selected = pair_rng.choice(len(pairs), size=N_COMPARISONS, replace=False)
    comparisons = label_pairs(designs, [pairs[i] for i in selected], noise_rng)
    records = []

    for iteration in range(N_STEPS + 1):
        # A fixed round seed keeps acquisition randomness matched across arms.
        bo = strategies.map(
            study_data.model_copy(update={"seed": replicate * 100 + iteration})
        )
        bo.tell(designs, preferences=comparisons)
        utility = latent_utility(designs[inputs.get_keys()].to_numpy())
        recommended = bo.predict(designs)["utility_pred"].to_numpy().argmax()
        records.append(
            {
                "feedback": feedback,
                "replicate": replicate,
                "iteration": iteration,
                "best_measured": float(utility.max()),
                "recommended": float(utility[recommended]),
            }
        )
        if iteration == N_STEPS:
            break

        new_design = bo.ask()[inputs.get_keys()].copy()  # qLogNEI
        new_design["labcode"] = f"measurement_{len(designs)}"
        designs = pd.concat([designs, new_design], ignore_index=True)
        pairs = list(combinations(range(len(designs)), 2))
        if feedback == "random pairs":
            selected = pair_rng.choice(len(pairs), size=N_COMPARISONS, replace=False)
        else:
            # Reuse the fitted GP to score pairs of measured designs.
            bo.acquisition_function = qEUBO(n_mc_samples=64)
            values = [
                bo.calc_acquisition(
                    designs.iloc[list(pair)][inputs.get_keys()], combined=True
                ).item()
                for pair in pairs
            ]
            selected = np.argsort(values)[-N_COMPARISONS:]
        new_comparisons = label_pairs(designs, [pairs[i] for i in selected], noise_rng)
        comparisons = pd.concat([comparisons, new_comparisons], ignore_index=True)
    return records
```

The qEUBO policy takes the two highest-scoring pairs, scored separately with
`combined=True`. Those two queries are a greedy selection, rather than a
jointly optimized set of comparisons. Pairs can be queried again in later
rounds with fresh judgment noise. Initial data and judgment-noise streams are
matched across policies within each replicate.

```{python}
study_results = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        record
        for replicate in range(N_REPLICATES)
        for feedback in ["random pairs", "qEUBO pairs"]
        for record in run_bo(feedback, replicate)
    ]
)
study_results.loc[study_results["iteration"] == N_STEPS].groupby("feedback")[
    ["best_measured", "recommended"]
].mean().round(3)
```

The left panel scores the best design measured so far. The right panel scores
the measured design with the highest posterior mean utility: finding a good
design and recognizing it are distinct parts of preference-based BO.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, metric, title in zip(
    axes,
    ["best_measured", "recommended"],
    ["Best measured design", "Model recommendation"],
):
    for feedback, group in study_results.groupby("feedback", sort=False):
        summary = group.groupby("iteration")[metric].agg(["mean", "std"])
        (line,) = ax.plot(summary.index, summary["mean"], marker="o", label=feedback)
        ax.fill_between(
            summary.index,
            summary["mean"] - summary["std"],
            (summary["mean"] + summary["std"]).clip(upper=0),
            color=line.get_color(),
            alpha=0.15,
        )
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", linestyle=":", label="true optimum")
    ax.set(xlabel="New experiments", title=title, xticks=range(N_STEPS + 1))
    ax.grid(alpha=0.2)
axes[0].set_ylabel("True utility (simulation only)")
axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Lines show the mean over ten replicates; shading shows one standard deviation.
This small synthetic example illustrates how comparison choices affect the
model and subsequent experiments; it does not establish a general winner.
